passages.happening:
In the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year, Nebuchadnezzar marched against Jerusalem with his whole army and besieged it (verse 1). ‘And on the ninth day of the fourth month of Zedekiah’s eleventh year, the city was breached’ (verse 2). The officials of the king of Babylon came in and sat in the Middle Gate (verse 3).

Zedekiah and all the soldiers saw them and fled by night through the king's garden, by the gate between the two walls, toward the Arabah (verse 4). The Chaldean army overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho and brought him to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, who passed sentence on him (verse 5). At Riblah the king of Babylon had Zedekiah's sons and the nobles of Judah killed, and then blinded Zedekiah and bound him in bronze chains to take him to Babylon (verses 6 and 7). The chapter states this in a line, and these notes go no further.

The Chaldeans burned the king's palace and the people's houses and broke down the walls of Jerusalem (verse 8). Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, carried the rest of the people to Babylon (verse 9). But he left some of the poorest people, who owned nothing, in the land of Judah, and gave them vineyards and fields (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The siege began about January 588 BC, and the wall was breached in July of 587 or 586 BC. Scholars divide over the year because ancient ways of counting a king's years can be reckoned more than one way. The same events are told in 2 Kings 25 and again in Jeremiah 52.

The Babylonian officers in verse 3 bear real Babylonian names and titles, though the Hebrew is hard to divide. In 2007 a cuneiform tablet in the British Museum, dated about 595 BC, was found to mention a chief official named Nabu-sharrussu-ukin, whom many scholars take to be the Nebo-sarsekim of this chapter, though some question the match.

Riblah was Nebuchadnezzar's headquarters in the north. Everything Jeremiah had warned Zedekiah of came to pass, and the end of David's reigning line in Jerusalem came in a single day.

The poorest of the land, who had owned nothing, were given the fields. The great reversal began in judgment.
passages.later: Lamentations grieves for the captured king: ‘The LORD’s anointed, the breath of our life, was captured in their pits’ (Lamentations 4:20). Ezekiel had said of Zedekiah, ‘I will bring him to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans; yet he will not see it’ (Ezekiel 12:13).
passages.hard:
Jeremiah told Zedekiah he would not die by the sword but would die in peace and be mourned (34:4-5). How does that fit this chapter?

The tension is real. Zedekiah was not killed by the sword; he was blinded and held in Babylon until his death (52:11). Some interpreters read the promise as meaning a natural death rather than execution, with mourning, which the prophecy does describe. Others think the promise was conditional, part of the offer that would have been kept if Zedekiah had surrendered, and his refusal changed the outcome. A third view notes that Ezekiel 12:13 said Zedekiah would be brought to Babylon but would not see it, which fits his blinding exactly.

What was done to Zedekiah and his sons was a conqueror's cruelty. The chapter reports it; it does not call it good.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Every warning Jeremiah gave came true in a single day. Ask what warning you have been given that you are still treating as unlikely. And ask what it means that the poorest people, who had nothing, were left with the fields.

passages.t: Jeremiah set free, and a promise to Ebed-melech
passages.happening:
Nebuchadnezzar had given orders about Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan (verse 11): ‘Take him, look after him, and do not let any harm come to him; do for him whatever he says’ (verse 12). So the Babylonian officers had Jeremiah brought out of the courtyard of the guard and handed him to Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, to take him home. And he stayed among the people (verses 13 and 14).

While Jeremiah was still confined, the word of the LORD had come to him for Ebed-melech the Cushite (verses 15 and 16). God would bring disaster on the city, but he would rescue Ebed-melech on that day, and he would not be handed to the men he feared (verse 17). ‘For I will surely rescue you so that you do not fall by the sword. Because you have trusted in Me, you will escape with your life like a spoil of war’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The Babylonians knew Jeremiah had urged surrender, and they treated him well. Their kindness was not a reward God promised, and the next chapter shows Jeremiah choosing to stay with the poor in Judah rather than go to comfort in Babylon.

Gedaliah son of Ahikam came from the family of Shaphan, who had served Josiah and protected Jeremiah before. Babylon would soon make him governor.

The promise to Ebed-melech is placed here, out of time order, so that the fall of the city is followed by the rescue of the man who rescued Jeremiah. To escape with your life like a spoil of war meant to come out of the disaster with nothing but your life, and that as a prize.
passages.later: Ebed-melech had pulled Jeremiah from the cistern (Jeremiah 38:10-13). A psalm says, ‘The LORD redeems His servants, and none who take refuge in Him will be condemned’ (Psalm 34:22).
passages.asks: Ebed-melech was rescued because he trusted God and acted when others would not. Ask what act of trust might be asked of you in a falling city. And ask whether you can receive your life itself as a gift when everything else is gone.
